core: Interfaith relations as dialogue and cooperation across religious boundaries
What interfaith dialogue is: structured conversation in which participants listen, learn, and share their own faith
Goals of dialogue: mutual understanding, reducing prejudice, cooperation on shared concerns, peacebuilding
Forms of interfaith work: dialogue groups, scriptural reasoning, shared service projects, interfaith councils, interfaith education
History: the 1893 World's Parliament of Religions as an early landmark; late-20th-century vocabulary; post-9/11 growth of interfaith organizations
What dialogue is NOT: not conversion, not syncretism, not relativism
Scholarly perspectives: promise and critiques (disputed prejudice reduction, flattening difference, imbalance of voices), attributed and neutral
Interfaith relations as the practical face of pluralism (reference to sibling topic religious-diversity)
supporting: The Pluralism Project's diversity-versus-pluralism framing ('the energetic engagement with diversity')
Exclusivism/inclusivism/pluralism taxonomy as scholarly context for dialogue
Documented variety of interfaith organizations and programs
outOfScope: Religious diversity as a social fact (sibling topic religious-diversity)
Religion and politics in depth (sibling topic religion-and-politics)
In-depth profiles of specific interfaith organizations
Religious advocacy or evaluation of any tradition's truth

claims.claim: 'Interfaith' and 'interreligious' are late-twentieth-century terms for dialogue, understanding, and cooperation across religious traditions; interfaith movements are premised on respecting each tradition's distinctiveness, not on creating a new faith.

Interfaith dialogue is structured conversation in which participants listen to and learn from people of other faiths as well as share their own — bringing one's own faith into genuine encounter with the faith of a neighbor.

Interfaith cooperation includes practical partnership across traditions on shared concerns — such as growing inequality, rising violence in cities, and climate change — in which participants explain their concerns in their own terms, citing different scriptures or teachings, yet work together.

After September 11, 2001, conversations about interfaith dialogue and the need to understand the faith of others gained new urgency, and several interfaith organizations were founded in the years that followed.

The 1893 World's Parliament of Religions, held in Chicago as part of the World's Columbian Exposition, lasted seventeen days in September 1893, brought together some four hundred men and women representing forty-one denominations and religious traditions, and marked the first formal gathering of representatives of Eastern and Western spiritual traditions; the Parliament of the World's Religions describes it as the birthplace of the worldwide interfaith movement.

The 1893 Parliament's stated aims — to promote friendly conference and mutual good understanding among people of diverse faiths while explicitly not seeking to foster 'the temper of indifferentism' and not striving to achieve any formal and outward unity — show that the early interfaith movement framed dialogue as preserving distinctiveness rather than erasing it.

Philosophical scholarship commonly divides responses to religious diversity into exclusivism, inclusivism, and pluralism; religious pluralists deny the primacy of any one religion, and scholars dispute whether acknowledging religious diversity reduces prejudice or leads to tolerance.

The Pluralism Project frames pluralism as 'the energetic engagement with diversity' — not diversity alone and not mere tolerance — with dialogue as the language of that engagement; interfaith relations is the practical face of pluralism.

The Pluralism Project documents a wide range of interfaith organizations and practices — dinner dialogues, interfaith councils, shared service projects, youth and university education programs, and peace walks — illustrating the forms interfaith work takes on the ground.

Scriptural reasoning is an interfaith practice in which Christians, Jews, Muslims, and members of other traditions meet in groups to study their sacred scriptures and oral traditions together; it was originally developed by theologians and religious philosophers and has spread beyond academic circles.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether interfaith dialogue and the acknowledgment of religious diversity actually reduce prejudice and lead to tolerance.
positions: The Pluralism Project describes mutual understanding and the reduction of prejudice as goals that dialogue serves, and interfaith organizations act on that premise.

The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy reports that the question whether acknowledged religious diversity can lead to religious tolerance is itself disputed, with some scholars skeptical that awareness of diversity reliably reduces prejudice.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents reduced prejudice as a goal of dialogue (attributed to the Pluralism Project) and separately notes the scholarly dispute about whether it is achieved (attributed to the SEP), without adjudicating.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether interfaith and comparative engagement can distort the traditions it brings together.
positions: Practitioners frame dialogue as respecting each tradition's distinctiveness (Pluralism Project; 1893 Parliament's stated aims).

Mikel Burley, cited in the SEP, criticizes generalizing approaches that downplay 'the particularities of historically and geographically distinct conceptions of God' in actual lived religions; John Schellenberg, also cited there, notes the field's continuing focus on theistic and especially classical Christian sources.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports these critiques neutrally and attributed (the risk of flattening difference; imbalance in which traditions' voices dominate), as scholarly debate rather than a verdict.

sourceRecords.title: 1893 Chicago: The Birthplace of the Interfaith Movement — Parliament of the World's Religions
sourceRecords.notes: Official organizational history page. Read via an Internet Archive capture of 2026-06-19; canonical URL registered.
